newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa blesses new nuns joining her Order.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa blesses new nuns joining her Order.

text.p: Mother Teresa met new members of her Missionaries of Charity religious order on Thursday, and her doctors said she was pleased to be doing better after life-saving surgery last week.
"We were happy to see her walk a little...she is happy that she is doing a little better and working hard...," a panel of doctors treating Mother Teresa said.
Mother Teresa took a few steps on Wednesday for the first time since surgery last Friday to clear two blocked arteries.

Two busloads of new members of the order founded by the 1979 Nobel Peace laureate met Mother Teresa to receive her blessing, said officials at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre, where she is being treated.
"They visited Mother Teresa for about half-an-hour," witnesses at the hospital said.
But doctors cautioned that she was still not out of danger.
Thursday's noon medical bulletin said: "Mother Teresa is not all that stable as yet. We truly do not have any estimate of her time of recovery. We could still encounter setbacks and complications."
Clinic administrator A.K. Chatterjee added: "It is a very very fragile equilibirum we are trying to maintain with regard to her medical parameters."
"Even though she made slight improvement yesterday and took a few steps, she is not at all out of danger," the bulletin quoted American Dr Patricia Aubanel as saying.
Doctors said they hoped to release Mother Teresa by the weekend.
An earlier bulletin had said Mother Teresa, 86, had gained strength, and her condition was improving.
The bulletin described the legendary missionary, who has devoted her life to the poor, destitute and dying, as "looking fresh" after a good night's sleep.
"She is cheerful," a clinic official told Reuters. He said she sat in a chair and said prayers after taking morning tea.

Mother Teresa's post-operative condition was complicated by an irregular heartbeat, bronchial pneumonia and long-standing kidney and lung problems. Last Friday marked her third round of heart-related surgery in five years.
A four-year-old boy who brought Mother Teresa a large get-well card was not permitted to meet her.
"I'm praying for Mother Teresa's health," said Steven Ebert, the son of an American volunteer worker at one of the order's homes for the destitute in Calcutta.
Doctors believe her recovery will take a long time and say Mother Teresa, who was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989, may never be as active as before.
Dr Tarun Praharaj, a member of her medical panel, said she was impatient to leave the clinic and return to her work with the poor. "I'm quite strong. I want to go home," he quoted her as saying.
Despite numerous health problems, Mother Teresa has kept a hectic schedule as head of her religious order and has travelled widely. The order's 4,500 members run 456 homes in 111 nations.
